---
title: Build a plugin
description: How to choose between a PLUGIN.md document, a remote plugin and a bundled TypeScript plugin, which repositories to clone, and the order of work from your first tool to a marketplace listing.
icon: Hammer
---

A plugin connects PKU Harness to one campus service, or adds one feature to the app. Each plugin
offers a set of _tools_: small, typed operations such as "list free classrooms" or "show my card
balance". The AI assistant and the user's own taps both call the same tools.

Writing a plugin therefore comes down to three jobs. You find out how the service answers
requests, you wrap those requests in tools, and, where it helps, you add a widget or a screen.

This section assumes you can read YAML or TypeScript and use a terminal. You don't need to know
the app's internals.

## Choose the kind

There are three kinds of plugin. Most people should write the first one.

A **plugin document** is a folder with a `PLUGIN.md` file. Its tools are written as YAML steps
with small, safe expressions, and the app interprets them on the phone. You publish it with
`git push`, and students install and update it from a link. Use it for most campus
integrations: requests to campus or public websites, extraction of the data you need, and the
user's campus session when a service requires sign-in. Start with the
[quickstart](/en/docs/build/quickstart), then read [Declarative plugins](/en/docs/build/declarative-plugins).
You can also [write it with the AI](/en/docs/build/ai-authoring) inside the app.

A **remote plugin** is a server you run yourself. It speaks the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a
standard way for AI apps to call tools over HTTP, using the Streamable HTTP transport. You can
write it in any language. Updates go out when you deploy the server; no app release is involved.
Use it for your own service, for heavy work, or for anything that needs general-purpose code.
Start from [`templates/remote-plugin`](/en/docs/build/remote-plugin).

A **bundled plugin** is a TypeScript module, written with zod and React Native, that ships inside
the app. It reaches users only with app releases, so open an issue before you start. Use it for
the app's own features (dashboard, schedule, scheduler, memory, model providers and so on) and for
integrations the plugin language can't express yet. Start with
[`definePlugin`](/en/docs/build/bundled-plugin).

| | Plugin document | Remote plugin | Bundled plugin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Written in | YAML steps and expressions | Any language (MCP) | TypeScript |
| Runs on | The phone, interpreted by the app | Your server | The phone, inside the app |
| How updates reach users | `git push` | Deploy your server | App release |

The official campus integrations classrooms, campus-events, grades, canteen, shuttle and notices
are already plugin documents. The other official integrations are still TypeScript, and we are
porting them one at a time.

## The order of work [#the-path]

<Steps>
<Step>

### Read the concepts

Four pages set the rules every plugin follows: [Plugins](/en/docs/concepts/plugins),
[Tools and effects](/en/docs/concepts/tools-and-effects), [Permissions](/en/docs/concepts/permissions)
and [Security](/en/docs/concepts/security). Read them first, because the review checks your plugin
against them.

</Step>
<Step>

### Find the protocol

You need to know which addresses the service uses and what it sends back. If
[`pkucli`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pkucli) already talks to the service, port its code and
credit the file you used. [Porting from pkucli](/en/docs/build/porting-from-pkucli) explains how.

</Step>
<Step>

### Write the tools

Write one tool per operation. Declare its effect honestly, put limits on every input, and write the
description for the model. For a plugin document, see
[Declarative plugins](/en/docs/build/declarative-plugins). For code, see
[Tools and schemas](/en/docs/build/tools).

</Step>
<Step>

### Add UI

A plugin document can add generative-UI widgets and screens (described as JSON and drawn by the
app), Settings rows and slash commands. A bundled plugin can also add native screens. See
[UI contributions](/en/docs/build/ui) and [Languages](/en/docs/build/i18n).

</Step>
<Step>

### Test

Each kind has its own tools. For plugin documents, `bun run plugin validate|test` checks the files
and replays recorded responses. For TypeScript logic, use `bun test`. To exercise the assistant's
loop without an API key, use the mock model. To try a remote plugin, use the demo remote plugin.
[Testing](/en/docs/build/testing) covers all four.

</Step>
<Step>

### Publish

Share the install link, then list the plugin in the marketplace. See
[Publishing](/en/docs/build/publishing), and in the marketplace section the
[manifest reference](/en/docs/marketplace/manifest) and the [submit flow](/en/docs/marketplace/publishing).

</Step>
</Steps>

## Repositories you need

Start with [`pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins). It
holds the SDK and the plugin language, the author command-line tool (`bun run plugin`), the
official plugin documents and bundled plugins, the marketplace registry, and the remote-plugin
template and examples.

You need [`pkuinfo/pku-harness`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness), the app itself, only to
run a bundled plugin on a phone or emulator. A plugin document doesn't need it until you want to
try campus requests for real.

[`pkuinfo/pkucli`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pkucli) is a set of Rust command-line tools for PKU
services. Use it as a reference for how each service's protocol works.

```bash
mkdir pku-info && cd pku-info
git clone https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins.git     # SDK, plugins, registry, template
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness.git   # only to run bundled plugins in the app
cd pku-harness-plugins && bun install && bun test
```

<Callout title="No npm packages">
  The SDK and the plugins are not published to npm. You use them straight from the GitHub
  repository: work inside a checkout of `pku-harness-plugins`, whose bun workspace and
  `tsconfig.json` resolve `@pku-harness/sdk` to `packages/sdk/src`. The app pulls in the same
  repository as the git submodule `plugins/`. Remote plugins don't need the SDK at all.
</Callout>

## Ground rules (from CONTRIBUTING.md)

1. **Tools are the API.** Give each tool a clear Chinese `title`, which users see, and a
   `description` written for the model that says when and how to use it. Validate every input:
   with `input` fields in a plugin document, with zod in a bundled plugin, and with JSON Schema in
   a remote plugin.
2. **Declare effects honestly.** A read-only tool sets `effect: read` (plugin documents and bundled
   plugins) or `readOnlyHint: true` (MCP). A tool that changes state, spends money or posts publicly
   must say so.
3. **Never ask for campus passwords.** Credentials stay on the user's phone.
4. **Return data, not instructions.** The model treats tool results as data.
5. **Declare what you reach.** In a plugin document, list `campus`, `network` and `abilities`;
   `requires` is derived from them. In code, list `requires`. Don't depend on a shell or a file
   system on the phone.
6. **Port campus protocols from pkucli** when it already implements them, and credit the source.
7. **Write both languages.** A plugin document has an `i18n.en` section. A bundled plugin needs an
   English overlay for every user-facing manifest string, and a `src/strings.ts` table for the text
   in its screens and widgets.
